title: Do You Actually Qualify for a Japanese University?
summary: Japan requires 12 years of prior schooling. If your country's system is shorter, there are official routes around it — and one is not a language school.
body_html:
This question comes before every other question about studying in Japan, and it is the one most guides skip: are you eligible to enter a Japanese university at all?

The rule is 12 years of schooling. [source:1] If your home system runs 12 years and you finished it, you qualify. [source:1] You can stop reading this and go choose a school. If it does not, you are in a situation with several official answers — and picking the wrong one wastes a year.

What the 12 year rule actually says [source:1]

The qualifying condition is completing 12 years of school education abroad. [source:1]

The ministry adds a definition that matters more than it looks: this means completing the twelfth year of the regular school education system of that country. [source:1] And it says plainly that whether your course was regular school education, and which year of it you completed, should be confirmed with that country's embassy. [source:1]

Read that as an instruction rather than a disclaimer. The ministry is telling you it will not adjudicate your home system's structure from a webpage — the embassy will. If your case is at all unusual, that is where the answer lives, and it is free to ask.

If your system is shorter than 12 years [source:1]

This is the common case for applicants from a number of countries, and it has a defined fix.

Where the course completed is fewer than 12 years, you must additionally complete a designated preparatory education course, or a designated training institution course. [source:1] The ministry publishes the list of both. [source:1]

Two things follow that people get wrong.

Not any language school will do. The course has to be on the ministry's designated list. A school that teaches Japanese excellently but holds no designation cannot close this gap, and no amount of JLPT will substitute.

It is not only language schools on that list. University-attached centres are on it too, including the Tokyo University of Foreign Studies international student Japanese language education centre and the Osaka University Japanese language and culture education centre. [source:2] So are the Japan Student Services Organization's own Tokyo and Osaka Japanese language education centres. [source:2]

The other routes, which hardly anyone mentions

The 12 year rule is the main road, but the ministry lists several others. [source:1] If you are stuck, check whether one of these is yours before you assume you need two extra years.

A qualification examination abroad. Passing an examination abroad certifying attainment equivalent to completion of 12 years of schooling qualifies you, if you are 18 or over. [source:1] The same under-12-years condition applies — if the course behind it was shorter, the designated preparatory course is still needed. [source:1] Whether your examination counts as equivalent is, again, a question for the embassy. [source:1]

A designated 11-year course. [source:1] There is a published list of foreign school courses corresponding to Japanese upper secondary school, where the course is treated as 11 years or more. [source:1] If your school is on that list, you are qualified without the preparatory course.

That one is worth a careful look. The difference between needing a preparatory course and being on the designated list is a year of your life and a year of tuition.

Internationally accredited schools. Completing the 12 year course of an institution accredited by WASC, CIS, ACSI, NEASC, Cognia or COBIS qualifies you. [source:1] Schools accredited under CIS's former name, ECIS, also count. [source:1]

If you went to an international school, start here rather than with your national system's year count.

Routes inside Japan. If you are already in Japan, graduating from an upper secondary school or a secondary education school qualifies you. [source:1] So does completing the upper secondary department of a special needs school, or the third year of a college of technology. [source:1] There is also a designated-institution route for facilities in Japan treated as equivalent to foreign upper secondary schools. [source:1]

The equivalency examination. Passing Japan's upper secondary school graduation equivalency examination qualifies you. [source:1] This is a route for people already in Japan with an incomplete secondary education, and it is rarely mentioned in study-abroad material because it sits outside the study-abroad industry.

How to work out which one is yours

  • Count the years of regular school education you completed, in your own system, to the year you finished. [source:1] Not the age you left — the year number.
  • If that is 12, you are qualified. [source:1] Go and choose a school.
  • If it is fewer, check the designated 11-year course list and the international accreditation list before accepting that you need a preparatory course. [source:1]
  • If neither applies, you need a designated preparatory education course or training institution course — and it has to be one on the ministry's list. [source:1]
  • If anything about your own system is ambiguous, ask your country's embassy, because the ministry explicitly directs you there. [source:1]

Do this before you shortlist schools, not after. A school cannot tell you whether your home education qualifies, and a school that implies it can has told you something useful about itself.

What the designated preparatory course actually is, and which of the schools we cover hold the designation, is set out in the designated preparatory course explained. If you already know you need one, the Sendagaya group comparison covers one such school's course in detail. For which entrance exam your target then requires, see JLPT or EJU.

Eligibility rules and the designated lists are published by the Ministry of Education and change; the pages linked below are the authority. This page summarises them and is not advice — individual cases are decided by the institution you apply to, and your own embassy is the reference for your home system.

claims_without_sources: 指定準備教育課程の現行校数 —— 一覧は公表されているが、文科省は「◯校」という数え方をしていない。自分で行を数えれば当方の集計になるため、数を書かず、読者に関係する校名を挙げるに留めた。
どの国の学制が何年かという具体例 —— 国ごとに異なり、文科省自身が「各国の大使館等に問い合わせよ」としている。特定の国名と年数を書けば、当方が判定したことになってしまうため書いていない。
11年以上の指定課程一覧・国際的評価団体認定校一覧の具体的な掲載校 —— 一覧の存在と参照先は出典どおりだが、各一覧の中身は確認していないため列挙していない。
高等学校卒業程度認定試験の受験資格・実施時期 —— 文部科学省の別ページの管轄であり、本記事の出典からは確認できないため触れていない。
準備教育課程を修了した場合の進学実績・合格率 —— 公表されていない。
